meta.title: The Brand Mapping Strategy: Design, Build, and Accelerate Your Brand
meta.author: Leland, Karen.

sentences: This book, *"The Brand Mapping Strategy"* by Karen Tiber Leland, aims to help **entrepreneurs, business owners, and CEOs** build and **accelerate their brands** by design, not default.
Leland, a branding and marketing strategist, shares insights, **proven strategies**, and **best practices** to **gain influence** within companies or industries and become a **thought leader**.
The book provides **actionable techniques** for designing, building, and accelerating personal, team, and business brands.
It is praised by various leaders for its practical advice on **raising one's profile**, **transforming self-portrayal**, **opening doors to opportunities**, and inspiring teams.

parts.title: HOW TO USE THIS BOOK FOR MAXIMUM BENEFIT

sentences: The author shares personal experiences and advice on using her book, "The Brand Mapping Strategy," for **maximum benefit**.
She learned from her hula teacher, Kawaikapuokalani Frank Hewett, that **"All knowledge is not learned in just one school."**
This applies to branding, meaning her book offers valuable insights but isn't the only source of truth.
She encourages readers to **"take what you like and leave the rest"** and emphasizes the book's modular structure, allowing readers to focus on relevant sections.
Real-life examples are included, with client names used with permission or altered to protect privacy.
The author suggests the book can be used for **emergency measures, a complete read-through, or as a yearly brand review**, encouraging readers to customize their approach.
The author, Karen Tiber Leland, works with CEOs, executives, and entrepreneurs to **develop stronger personal, business, and team brands**.
She wrote the book to reach a wider audience beyond her direct consulting capacity.
She provides her **contact information and website** for additional resources like blogs, articles, ebooks, webinars, and online training related to social media, marketing, and branding.
The overarching message is to make the book **work for the individual reader and their brand**, emphasizing a flexible and personalized approach.

parts.title: The Brand Mapping Strategy: Beyond the Surface

sentences: Building a **website** without a clear **brand message** is a common mistake; your **brand** should always drive the website design.
The author's mantra is "Brand Before You Build," emphasizing the need to establish a **clearly articulated brand and messages** before developing a platform.
Many people think of branding as the "three Ls"—**look**, **logo**, and **line** (tagline/elevator pitch)—but these are just the surface.
True branding requires articulating **seven core brand elements** for a deeper understanding and representation.

These seven core elements are the **Anchor Statement**, **Unique Branding Proposition**, **Brand Tone and Temperament**, **Brand Energy**, **Signature Story**, **Signature Services**, and **Brand Enhancers and Reducers**.
They provide a comprehensive framework for defining a brand, whether personal, team, or business.
A **strong website** is crucial for credibility and customer acquisition; a journalist won't use experts with poor websites, and a dentist lost clients due to an unprofessional online presence.

It also stresses the importance of **website quality**, **color and design psychology**, **speedy navigation**, clear **calls to action**, **SEO**, and **responsive design** for modern, marketing-oriented websites, as well as **brand consistency** across all social media platforms.

parts.title: Understanding and Crafting Your Brand's Identity

sentences: The concept of **Brand Clarity** can be achieved through an **Anchor Statement** and **Unique Branding Proposition (UBB)**.
It begins with an anecdote highlighting the importance of clear communication, showing how a vague description of services can lead to disengagement.
The **Anchor Statement** is introduced as a brief, go-to description of what you do, designed to be easily understood and integrated into a listener's existing patterns.
It's not the "total picture" but a concise, multi-layered explanation that can be expanded upon in conversation.

Examples from clients like an M&A advisor, an agricultural company, and a knitting store owner demonstrate how these statements effectively convey their core offerings, results, and unique approaches.

The text emphasizes that a good Anchor Statement doesn't need to be "sexy" but rather **resonate with the audience** and be conversational, allowing for natural expansion on its **"Be, Do, Have"** elements.
The document then delves into the **Unique Branding Proposition (UBP)**, which answers the crucial question of "Why you?"

It highlights specific attributes that can contribute to a UBP, such as **specialized background, proprietary processes, unique talents, niche expertise, innovative solutions, or difficult-to-imitate offerings**.
An exercise helps individuals identify their UBP by rating their brand's attributes against audience needs and competitors.
This "Hot Zone" analysis helps pinpoint strengths to leverage.
The text also introduces **Brand Tone and Temperament** (brand personality) and **Brand Energy** (flair, aptitude, talents).
Understanding these elements is crucial for creating a **consistent brand identity** across all platforms, from logos and websites to overall messaging.

Finally, it presents **12 archetypal brand energies**—Advocate, Maker, Connector, Motivator, and Synthesizer being the first few detailed—to help individuals align their brand with their authentic strengths and craft a more effective brand-building strategy.

parts.title: Understanding Brand Energy, Signature Stories, and Strategic Implementation

sentences: **Brand Mapping Strategy** details how to **articulate your brand narrative** through seven core elements and then **implement a strategy** to communicate it.

It highlights various brand energies like the Integrator, who blends things to make them better (e.g., Susan Harrow, a media coach who creates **cohesive messages** from various sources), the Fixer, who sees problems as **opportunities for creative solutions** (e.g., Joanne’s father who cheerfully tackled daily problems), the Implementer, skilled at turning goals into **tangible actions** (e.g., Dana Aftab who meticulously plans trips and business operations), and the Visionary, who **imagines possibilities** and translates them into actionable ideas (e.g., Binta Niambi Brown, CEO innovating a new music business model).

Other brand energies include the Interpreter, who **adds value through new translations** (e.g., Kim Bromley, transforming written words), the Storyteller, who uses **powerful narratives** to inspire change (e.g., Dewitt Jones, using stories and visuals), the Facilitator, talented at guiding groups to **consensus** (e.g., Colleen Rudio, mediating group decisions), and the Mentor, who acts as a **trusted advisor** and supports others (e.g., Aaron Young, guiding entrepreneurs).

The text then delves into the **Signature Story**, emphasizing its authenticity, serendipity, and specific examples, noting five common story types: Rags to Riches, Beat the Bad, There and Back Again, Eyes on the Prize, and Awakening.

Finally, it introduces **Signature Services**—specific competencies or offers (e.g., Care 2 Communities converting shipping containers into clinics)—and **Brand Enhancers and Reducers**, utilizing a SWOT analysis framework (Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats) to assess current brand effectiveness and plan for improvement.

parts.title: The Brand Mapping Strategy & Social Media Impact

sentences: **Brand mapping strategies** and how to **measure success** are a **marathon, not a sprint**.
You need to define **evaluation criteria** (e.g., attracting new prospects, increasing credibility, generating cash) and track progress in **customers**, **credibility**, and **cash**.
The "blow dryer effect" is where what was once special becomes expected, so constant **updating** of your strategy is urged to remain **relevant**.
The second part of the text, "Your Personal Brand in Action," focuses on **social media**.
It highlights that social media has been around for a relatively **short time** but has a **huge impact** on branding and marketing.

Key findings show that social media **increases exposure** for businesses (90% of marketers), consumers use search engines **before buying** (89%), and **online peer recommendations** are more trusted than ads (78%).
Additionally, 43% of social media users have **purchased a product** after sharing or favoriting it.
An effective social media campaign has a **positive impact** on brand building.

parts.title: The Misguided Myths & Three Expressions of Personal Branding

sentences: The **misguided myths of personal branding** started with Tom Peters' 1997 article "The Brand Called You."
It highlights how personal branding has evolved, especially with the internet, becoming crucial for **CEO effectiveness, executive leadership, and career planning**.
However, several myths have emerged.
For instance, personal branding is **not a new phenomenon**, as historical figures like Napoleon Bonaparte had strong personal brands.
Your **reputation isn't your entire personal brand**, as online and offline perceptions can differ.
A personal brand is **not just about you**; a positive one benefits others, with research showing employees enjoy work more and feel empowered under good leaders.
Finally, a personal brand is **not always good**, as some individuals have disruptive or destructive brands.
The **three expressions of your personal brand** are visual, intellectual, and emotional capital.
The **visual element** includes your **style of dress**, color/design choices for branding collateral, **headshot**, and social media backgrounds.
Clothes transmit social signals about sophistication, success, and credibility.
A professional headshot is crucial, with tips like **facing forward and smiling**, and removing distractions.

The **intellectual aspect** involves **brand sound bites**, a **branded biography** (show, don't tell; be bold without bragging), social media profiles (using character limits and keywords), and **content creation** (blogging, podcasting, videocasting, authoring a book).
The **emotional connection** is about what feelings you want your audience to experience, like joy, security, or excitement.
**When to rebrand** includes when your message or audience has changed, your collateral is outdated, or your reputation is damaged.

parts.title: Your C-Suite and CEO Brand: Building Reputation and Thought Leadership

sentences: **Building a strong executive brand** for CEOs and C-Suite members is no longer a luxury but a **necessity in our digital world**.
A study from 2003 even found that **48% of a company's reputation** is linked to its CEO.
The key is to create a **"parallel brand"** that perfectly blends personal and company brands.

To be effective, this parallel brand must **complement the business**, be **authentic**, **positive or captivating**, **obvious internally and externally**, and **enhance both the CEO's and the business's reputation**.

Benefits of a strong CEO reputation include attracting employees (77%), motivating them to stay (70%), and contributing to market value (44%), not to mention **attracting investors**, **generating positive media**, and **crisis protection**.
A **four-part matrix** for building a C-Suite/CEO brand includes: **reputation management**, **thought leadership**, **content marketing**, and **executive presence**.

For **reputation management**, it's crucial to **claim your name online** (registering URLs, securing social media handles) and **monitor search engines** (setting Google Alerts, pushing down undesirable results with new content, creating public profiles).
The importance of being a **"Social CEO"** is highlighted, with a 2014 survey showing that **social media participation improves communication, brand image, transparency, and morale**.
**LinkedIn is a must-have** for executives, and a strong profile with a headshot, job history, summary, skills, and recommendations is essential.
The chapter stresses that a CEO's online presence, like their LinkedIn profile, can be a **deciding factor** in key interactions.

parts.title: Breaking the Vicious Cycle: Commitment-Based Change and Continuous Brand Improvement

sentences: Companies trying to become **brand-centric** often enter a **vicious cycle of change management**, frequently failing due to lack of **senior management alignment**, **insufficient resources**, **poor structure**, or not using **external expertise**.
It details stages like **promises made**, then **something coming up** that compromises them, leading to **lack of communication**, **lack of ownership**, and eventually **anger and frustration**.
This cycle can repeat with **re-plans and re-commitments** but with lower momentum and higher skepticism.
To break this cycle, the **Process of Commitment-Based Change** is more effective.

This process involves **engaging the C-Suite** (Phase 1) to ensure top-level commitment, **building awareness** (Phase 2) across the organization to understand the current state, **educating and training** (Phase 3) staff and management to be brand ambassadors, **practicing continuous improvement** (Phase 4) through structured groups, and finally, **creating reward and recognition** (Phase 5) systems to reinforce brand-centric behaviors.

A key tool for continuous improvement is the **Continuous Brand Improvement (CBI) Process**, which is a six-step methodology to tackle systematic issues and align a company's functions with its brand promise.
It also introduces **Team Branding**, which helps intact or project teams define their own brand, strategy, and code of conduct for greater alignment and effectiveness.
